query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high configurational entropy and resultant sluggish diffusion in equiatomic 5-metal nanoparticles primarily stabilize the single-phase solid solution structure across catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures (473–1923 K, even under reactive atmospheres), unless surface and interfacial energy effects become pronounced at very small sizes.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles (5–20 nm) composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: In situ high-temperature synchrotron-based diffraction and spectroscopy while exposing the nanoparticles to catalytic/thermoelectric reactive environments with temperature ramping from 473 K up to ~1923 K.
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are size-selected and measured in a controlled reactive atmosphere that mimics catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions; temperature is precisely controlled during the in situ measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice parameters, peak broadening (indicative of phase changes or ordering), and the spatial distribution of constituent elements (tracking any onset of segregation or local chemical fluctuations).
generation.mechanism: High mixing entropy leads to sluggish diffusion and retards phase segregation, thus maintaining a single-phase solid solution even at high temperatures. However, at the nanoscale, enhanced surface and interfacial energies could, under reactive conditions, locally lower kinetic barriers and drive elemental partitioning if they become significant.
generation.predicted_outcome: If high configurational entropy dominates, the in situ measurements will show a largely stable lattice (with only minor thermal expansion) and a uniform elemental distribution across the temperature range. A deviation (e.g., emergence of secondary phases or compositional heterogeneities) is expected only if interfacial effects overcome the entropic stabilization, potentially occurring in nanoparticles with particularly high surface-to-volume ratios.
generation.baseline: The initial state is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with equiatomic composition at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The prediction should hold under reactive conditions representative of operational catalytic and thermoelectric environments. If nanoparticles are substantially smaller than 5 nm or if the reactive environment significantly alters surface energies, these conditions may drive segregation even at lower temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold and the relative contribution of surface energy effects versus entropic stabilization remain uncertain; additional measurements are needed to quantify the interplay of these factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) on size-selected 5–20 nm equiatomic nanoparticles while subjecting them to a controlled reactive ambience and a temperature ramp from 473 K to ~1923 K. Compare diffraction patterns and elemental maps over the temperature range.
measurements: Temperature-dependent XRD to monitor lattice parameter shifts, peak splitting, or new phase formation.
In situ XAS or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to detect any local elemental segregation or chemical ordering.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If secondary phases or significant elemental segregation (i.e., clear deviations from a uniform solid solution) are observed at temperatures well below 1000 K, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy primarily governs stability through sluggish diffusion would be falsified.

To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. decision.trend: Early studies on five-component refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 and NbMoCrTiAl) used vacuum arc melting, hot isostatic pressing, or spark plasma sintering to consolidate near-equiatomic multi-principal systems. These works focused on high-temperature mechanical performance, demonstrating that high mixing entropy often stabilizes single-phase or predominantly single-phase microstructures in bulk form. Subsequent research (e.g., on HfNbTaTiZr and CrMoNbWV) examined more advanced powder metallurgy routes and sintering conditions, revealing that partial phase transformations (e.g., secondary phases such as Laves or oxides) can emerge at elevated temperatures, which degrade mechanical properties. Although the ‘sluggish diffusion’ and high mixing entropy concepts often delay phase segregation, the exact temperature bounds and environmental constraints for stability remain under active study. None of these works directly target nanoscale catalysts or thermoelectric materials over a broad temperature range, leaving a gap in understanding elemental partitioning, local chemical fluctuations, and structural evolution under catalytic or thermoelectric service conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite promising observations of high-entropy stabilization at the bulk scale, the fundamental mechanisms that govern how five-plus component nanoparticles maintain (or lose) structural and chemical homogeneity from 473 K up to ~1923 K under catalytic or thermoelectric conditions have not been systematically confirmed. Interfacial effects, short-range ordering, local segregation, and the role of reactive environments at high temperatures remain incompletely understood at the nanoscale.
decision.lever: Conduct in situ high-temperature synchrotron-based diffraction and spectroscopy on size-selected 5-metal nanoparticles (e.g., 5–20 nm) in reactive atmospheres up to ~1900 K, tracking lattice transformations and elemental distributions in real time
decision.why: Building on bulk high-entropy alloy results that emphasize sluggish diffusion and entropic stabilization, the next logical step is to directly observe any phase separation, compositional shifts, or morphological changes in nanoparticles exposed to catalytic or thermoelectric conditions. Such real-time measurements would test whether multi-metal entropic stabilization dominates at these extreme temperatures or if interfacial effects and environmental factors trigger unanticipated degradation. A contradiction—e.g., if marked chemical partitioning occurs well below 1000 K under relevant process conditions—would falsify the hypothesis that high configurational entropy alone controls nanoparticle stability.
